questions.q:
Five students of a Pune school each sketched the Moon on one date of the same month. The school calendar marks a full Moon on 5 October and the next full Moon on 3 November.
Dates sketched: 7 October, 12 October, 19 October, 23 October and 30 October.
The student who went out on 19 October saw no Moon at all, although the sky was clear, and wrote 'cloudy night' in her record.
(a) On which of these dates would the bright part be about a half circle, and is that date in Shukla Paksha or Krishna Paksha?
(b) Give the chapter's reason why no Moon was seen on 19 October, so that 'cloudy night' can be corrected.
(c) Rank the sketches of 7 October, 23 October and 30 October from the most to the least of the illuminated portion seen from the Earth.
(d) The school wants one sketch for a poster titled 'A gibbous Moon that will look bigger tomorrow'. Decide which date's sketch to use, and say why each of the other two dates in (c) does not fit.
questions.a: (a) 12 October, about a week after the full Moon; the bright part is shrinking, so it is Krishna Paksha. (b) 19 October is about two weeks after the full Moon, close to the new Moon day: the Moon is towards the Sun and only its non-illuminated half faces the Earth, so it cannot be seen even in a clear sky. (c) 7 October (only 2 days after a full Moon), then 30 October (4 days before the next full Moon), then 23 October (a crescent, a few days after the new Moon). (d) 30 October: it is gibbous and in the waxing period (heading to the 3 November full Moon), so it grows each night. 7 October is gibbous but waning, so it will look smaller tomorrow; 23 October is waxing but only a crescent, not gibbous.
s: (a) 12 October, Krishna Paksha
(b) near the new Moon: only the non-illuminated half faces the Earth
(c) 7 Oct, then 30 Oct, then 23 Oct
(d) 30 October, waxing gibbous; 7 Oct waning, 23 Oct a crescent

questions.q:
True or false? Correct the statement if it is false.

questions.a: False. The same half of the Moon always faces the Earth. On a new Moon day that half is simply the non-illuminated half, because the illuminated half faces the Sun, which lies behind the Moon as seen from the Earth.
s: verdict: false
the same half always faces the Earth; at new Moon it is the non-illuminated half

questions.q: In one complete cycle, from one full Moon to the next, the Moon is seen in the gibbous phase during ___ separate stretches of days (write a number).

At one moment the Moon is at the position where, seen from the Earth, exactly half of its illuminated portion is visible and the bright part is shrinking each night. Three observers look at the Moon at that same moment:
Observer P stands on the Earth.
Observer Q is in a spacecraft placed between the Sun and the Moon, looking at the Moon.
Observer R is in a spacecraft on the far side of the Moon from the Sun, looking at the Moon.
(a) Describe what each of P, Q and R sees. (3 marks)
(b) All three look at the same Moon at the same moment. What do their different views show about whether the Moon's shape changes? (1 mark)
(c) A classmate says: 'Only on this one day of the month is half of the Moon lit by the Sun.' Judge this using your answers. (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) P sees a half circle of brightness (the waning half Moon), because only part of the illuminated half faces the Earth. Q faces the side lit by the Sun, so Q sees the whole illuminated half: a full bright circle. R faces the side turned away from the Sun, so R sees only the non-illuminated half: a dark disc, like a new Moon. (b) The Moon is the same sphere for all three; only the part of its illuminated half that faces each observer differs. So the Moon's shape does not change; what we see changes with where we look from. (c) The classmate is wrong: on every day of the month one half of the Moon, the half facing the Sun, is lit (as Q's view shows). What is special about this day is only that the Earth sees half of that lit half.
s: P: half circle seen, part of the lit half faces the Earth
Q: whole lit half seen as a full circle
R: only the dark half seen, like a new Moon
the Moon's shape does not change, only the visible part of its lit half
judges the claim wrong: half the Moon is lit every day

questions.q:
In a dark room, Raju models the Moon with a ball on a stick and a lamp for the Sun; his head is the Earth.
(a) He holds the ball between his head and the lamp. What does he see of the ball, and which day of the Moon does this model?
(b) He then turns so the ball is on the side away from the lamp, but holds it low, so the shadow of his head falls on the ball. Using (a), explain whether this models a phase or a lunar eclipse.
questions.a: (a) He sees none of the lit portion, only the non-illuminated side of the ball faces him; this models the new Moon day (Amavasya). (b) It models a lunar eclipse, not a phase: his head plays the Earth, and the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is what causes a lunar eclipse. In (a) the dark ball was due to which side faced him, with no shadow involved, which is how phases really happen.
s: (a) only the unlit side seen; new Moon day
(b) head's shadow on the ball models a lunar eclipse, unlike the phase in (a)

questions.q:
A science-club notice makes two claims.
Claim 1: 'As the bright part of the Moon gets thinner after a full Moon, the Moon appears closer to the Sun in the sky each morning.'
Claim 2: 'This happens because the Moon itself shrinks in size and shape during that fortnight.'
Is the notice as a whole right, wrong or partly right? Explain each claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Claim 1 is correct: in the waning period, as the bright part shrinks, the Moon appears closer to the Sun at sunrise each day, and it is closest at the new Moon. Claim 2 is wrong: the Moon's shape never changes. Only the fraction of its illuminated half that faces the Earth changes as it revolves around the Earth, so what we see changes.
s: verdict: partly right
Claim 1 correct: the waning Moon appears closer to the Sun each morning
Claim 2 wrong: the Moon's shape does not change; the visible fraction of its lit half changes

(b) On about which date after 9 August will it last be a half circle, and in which Paksha? (1 mark)

(d) A hotel offers the club the nights of 12 to 21 August. Will every night meet the rule? Explain. (1 mark)
(e) The club wants a second trek around the next full Moon. On about which date should that trek be centred? (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) About 2 August, one week before the full Moon; the bright part is growing, so Shukla Paksha. (b) About 16 August, one week after the full Moon; the bright part is shrinking, so Krishna Paksha. (c) From about 2 to 16 August, about two weeks (about 15 nights). (d) No. After about 16 August the bright part is less than a half circle (crescent, Krishna Paksha), so the nights of about 17 to 21 August fail the rule. (e) The next full Moon is about 29.5 days after 9 August, around 7 to 8 September, so the trek should be centred there.

(b) about 16 August, Krishna Paksha
(c) about two weeks (about 15 nights)
(d) no: after about 16 August the Moon is a waning crescent
(e) next full Moon about 29.5 days later, around 7 to 8 September

questions.q:
Ishita in Bhopal kept a Moon diary, starting on the day after a full Moon.
Day 1 (sunrise): almost a full circle.
Day 4: bright part smaller than on Day 1. Label: 'waxing gibbous'.
Day 8: half circle, smaller than before.
Day 12: thin crescent. Label: 'Krishna Paksha'.
Day 15: Moon not seen in a clear sky. Note: 'New Moon: its illuminated half is turned towards the Earth.'
Her friend Arjun in Kolkata also recorded the Moon on Day 12 and wrote 'half circle'.
(a) One of the two labels (Day 4 or Day 12) is wrong. Find it and correct it.
(b) Correct the note written on Day 15.
(c) Predict the shape Ishita should see about a week after Day 15, and whether it will be growing or shrinking.
(d) Decide whose Day 12 entry, Ishita's or Arjun's, should be checked again. Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Day 4 label is wrong. After a full Moon the bright part shrinks, so it is a waning gibbous (Krishna Paksha), not waxing. (b) At new Moon the non-illuminated half faces the Earth; the illuminated half faces the Sun. (c) About a half circle, growing each night (waxing, Shukla Paksha). (d) Arjun's entry. On a given day people in different parts of the Earth see nearly the same phase, so the two entries cannot both be right; Ishita's sequence (half circle on Day 8, about a week after the full Moon, then shrinking) makes a thin crescent on Day 12 the consistent one.
s: (a) Day 4 label wrong: should be waning gibbous
(b) at new Moon the non-illuminated half faces the Earth
(c) half circle, growing (waxing)
(d) Arjun's entry: same phase everywhere on a day, and Ishita's sequence fits

(b) A crescent, less than half of the illuminated portion, since four days before the waxing half Moon the Moon had only recently passed the new Moon.

(b) a crescent, less than half

questions.q: Kabir says he saw a full Moon one night and a thin crescent on the very next evening. Show that this cannot happen.
questions.a: After a full Moon the bright part shrinks slowly over the waning period: it takes about a week to shrink from a full circle to a half circle. One day after the full Moon only a tiny change has happened, so the Moon still shows more than half of its illuminated portion (gibbous). A crescent (less than half) appears only after the half Moon, more than a week after the full Moon. So a crescent on the next evening is impossible.
s: full circle to half circle takes about a week
one day later the Moon is still gibbous (more than half)

questions.q:
A planetarium in Bengaluru drafted this notice of sky events for the coming year.
Event 1: a lunar eclipse on a full Moon day in March.
Event 2: a solar eclipse on a new Moon day in March, about two weeks after Event 1.
Event 3: a solar eclipse on a day when the Moon is a thin crescent, in May.
Event 4: a lunar eclipse on a new Moon day in September.
(a) Before anything else, decide which of the four events must be removed from the notice.
(b) Give the reason for removing each one.
(c) Explain why Event 2 can come about two weeks after Event 1.
(d) A visitor asks why the notice does not show an eclipse every month, since a full Moon and a new Moon come every month. Write the planetarium's reply.
questions.a: (a) Events 3 and 4 must be removed. (b) A solar eclipse can happen only on a new Moon day, so not on a crescent day (Event 3). A lunar eclipse can happen only on a full Moon day, so not on a new Moon day (Event 4). (c) A lunar eclipse needs a full Moon and a solar eclipse needs a new Moon; the Moon goes from full to new in about two weeks (the waning period), so the two can be about two weeks apart. (d) The Moon's orbit is slightly tilted with respect to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, so on most full Moon and new Moon days the Sun, Earth and Moon do not line up for an eclipse.
s: (a) removes Events 3 and 4
(b) solar only on new Moon; lunar only on full Moon
(c) full Moon to new Moon takes about two weeks
(d) small tilt of the Moon's orbit prevents monthly eclipses

So the full Moon is on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun all day. At noon, when the Sun is high up, the full Moon is on the other side of the Earth, below the horizon, so it cannot be overhead at the same time.

at sunrise the full Moon is setting in the West

questions.q:
A Kochi newspaper printed these moonrise times for five days in a row:
Day 1: 13:10
Day 2: 14:02
Day 3: 14:51
Day 4: 13:44
Day 5: 16:31
One of the five entries is a misprint. Neel, a Class 8 student, went out on Day 2 at 14:10, looked at the eastern sky and saw no Moon.
(a) Which entry is the misprint, and about what time should it be? Give your reason.
(b) Using Day 1 and Day 5, find the average daily delay, and give the chapter's reason for this delay.
(c) Explain why Neel saw no Moon on Day 2.
(d) The school club can hold a daytime Moon-watch at 3:30 p.m. on either Day 2 or Day 4. Decide which day to choose, using your answers to (a) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Day 4. Moonrise gets later each day, so it cannot be earlier than Day 3 (14:51). About 50 minutes after Day 3 gives about 15:41 (it also sits midway between 14:51 and 16:31). (b) (16:31 - 13:10) / 4 = 201 / 4 = about 50 minutes a day. The Moon moves ahead in its orbit while the Earth completes one rotation in 24 hours, so the Earth must rotate a little more to bring the Moon back to the same spot. (c) At 14:10 the Moon had risen only 8 minutes earlier; it takes about 30 minutes past moonrise to climb high enough to be seen. (d) Day 2. By 3:30 p.m. the Moon has been up for about 88 minutes, long enough to be seen. On Day 4 the corrected moonrise is about 15:41, so at 3:30 p.m. the Moon has not risen yet.
s: (a) Day 4 misprint; about 15:41, since moonrise is later each day
(b) about 50 minutes; Moon moves ahead in its orbit during one rotation
(c) only 8 minutes after moonrise; needs about 30 minutes to climb
(d) Day 2: Moon up for about 88 minutes; on Day 4 it has not risen

questions.q: Dev says, 'The Moon rises about 50 minutes later every day because the Earth spins more slowly at night.' Correct Dev's reason.
questions.a: The Earth's rotation does not slow down; it completes one rotation in 24 hours. The delay happens because the Moon moves ahead a little in its orbit around the Earth during that day, so the Earth has to rotate some more before the Moon appears in nearly the same spot in the sky.

A calendar app shows that sunrise in Indore changes by only a minute or so from one day to the next, while moonrise changes by about 50 minutes a day.
(a) Why does moonrise shift so much more than sunrise from day to day?
(b) On about which day of the Moon's cycle does the Moon rise closest to the time of sunrise? Give the reason.
(c) On about which day does it rise closest to the time of sunset? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The Moon moves ahead in its orbit around the Earth during each day, so the Earth must rotate a little more (about 50 minutes) to bring the Moon back to the same place in the sky; the Sun has no such daily jump. (b) Around the new Moon day, because then the Moon appears closest to the Sun in the sky, so it rises at nearly the same time as the Sun. (c) Around the full Moon day, because then the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun: it is setting in the West as the Sun rises, so it rises in the East at about the time the Sun sets.
s: (a) the Moon moves ahead in its orbit, so the Earth must turn about 50 minutes more
(b) new Moon day: Moon closest to the Sun in the sky
(c) full Moon day: Moon nearly opposite the Sun

questions.a: (a) The Moon does not rise with sunset: it rises about 50 minutes later each day, so on some days it rises in the afternoon (around 2 to 4 p.m.) or stays up after sunrise, and it is then in the sky while the Sun is up. (b) No. On Amavasya the Moon appears closest to the Sun and only its non-illuminated half faces the Earth, so it cannot be seen at any time of day.
s: (a) moonrise shifts about 50 minutes a day, so sometimes the Moon is up in daylight
(b) no: on Amavasya only the non-illuminated half faces the Earth

questions.q:
On a full Moon day in Nagpur the Moon rose at 6:10 p.m., close to sunset.
(a) Using the chapter's daily delay, estimate the moonrise time 7 days later. (1 mark)
(b) What shape will the Moon have by then, and where will it be at sunrise on the morning that follows that moonrise? (1 mark)
(c) Estimate the total delay in moonrise over one full cycle of 29.5 days, in hours. (1 mark)
(d) Use (c) to explain why, on some days of the month, moonrise falls in the afternoon. (1 mark)
(e) Using (c), predict roughly when the Moon will rise on the next full Moon day, and say why. (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) 7 x 50 = 350 minutes, about 5 hours 50 minutes later: 6:10 p.m. + 5 h 50 min = about midnight. (b) A waning half circle; it will be overhead at sunrise, which fits a Moon that rose around midnight. (c) 29.5 x 50 = 1475 minutes, about 24.6 hours, roughly one whole day. (d) Over the month the moonrise time slides through every hour of the clock, so on some days it lands in the afternoon (around 2 to 4 p.m.). (e) About 6:45 p.m. (between 6 and 7 p.m.), near sunset again: the total slip of about 24.6 hours is one full day plus about 35 minutes, so moonrise comes back to about 6:10 p.m. + 35 min.
s: (a) 350 minutes later, about midnight
(b) waning half Moon, overhead at sunrise
(c) 1475 minutes, about 24.6 hours
(d) moonrise slides through all hours, so some days fall in the afternoon
(e) about 6:45 p.m.: 24.6 h is one day plus about 35 minutes

(e) Name both changes from (a) to (c) that would change the number of Moon-phase cycles that fit into one year. (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) The day would become shorter, because the day is based on the Earth's rotation (the Sun returning to its highest position). The month and the year would not change in length, though each would hold more days. (b) The month would become longer, because the month is based on the cycle of the Moon's phases, which comes from the Moon's revolution around the Earth. (c) The year would become shorter, because the year is the cycle of seasons, set by the Earth's revolution around the Sun. (d) The month: it is observed through the Moon's phases, and with no reflected sunlight there would be no phases to watch. (e) Changes (b) and (c): the number of phase cycles in a year depends on both the month and the year.

(b) Twelve cycles of the Moon's phases take about 12 x 29.5 = 354 days, about 11 days less than the cycle of seasons.

(b) 12 phase cycles are about 354 days, about 11 days short

questions.q:
Zoya noted the dates of full Moons through one year (dates illustrative): 13 Jan, 12 Feb, 14 Mar, 13 Apr, 12 May, 11 Jun, 10 Jul, 9 Aug, 7 Sep, 7 Oct, 5 Nov, 4 Dec. The year was not a leap year.
(a) From 13 January to 4 December there are 325 days. Find the average gap between full Moons and name the unit of time this cycle is the basis of.
(b) Which motion causes this cycle?
(c) Zoya's year had 12 full Moons. Explain whether some other year could have 13.
(d) Her society wants a monthly 'full Moon walk' fixed on the 13th of every month. Decide whether this will work, using the data.
questions.a: (a) 325 days hold 11 gaps: 325 / 11 = about 29.5 days. This cycle of phases is the basis of the month. (b) The Moon's revolution around the Earth, which changes how much of its illuminated half faces the Earth. (c) Yes. Twelve cycles take about 12 x 29.5 = 354 days, about 11 days less than a 365-day year, so if the first full Moon falls in the first ten days or so of January, a thirteenth can still fit before 31 December. (d) It will not work. A full Moon comes about every 29.5 days, while calendar months average about 30.4 days, so the full Moon slides earlier through the month: the data move from the 13th in January to the 4th by December.
s: (a) about 29.5 days; basis of the month
(b) the Moon's revolution around the Earth
(c) yes: 12 cycles are 354 days, about 11 days short of the year
(d) no: the full Moon drifts earlier (13th to 4th in the data)

questions.q:
(a) Name the natural cycle on which the month is based, with its length.
(b) Using (a), find about how many such cycles fit into one cycle of seasons, and say why the answer is not a whole number.
questions.a: (a) The cycle of the Moon's phases, about 29.5 days. (b) 365.25 / 29.5 = about 12.4, so about 12 and a bit. The two cycles come from different motions (the Moon going round the Earth, the Earth going round the Sun), so one does not fit a whole number of times into the other.
s: (a) Moon's phases, about 29.5 days
(b) about 12.4; the cycles come from different motions

questions.q:
Imagine the Earth took 400 days to go once around the Sun, while the Earth's rotation and the Moon's phase cycle (29.5 days) stayed the same (illustrative).
(a) Which of the day, the month and the year would change?
(b) About how many cycles of the Moon's phases would then fit into one year?
(c) Would a lunar year of 12 phase cycles then fall short of the seasons by more or by less than it does now? Show the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Only the year, which is set by the Earth's revolution around the Sun; the day (rotation) and the month (phase cycle) stay the same. (b) 400 / 29.5 = about 13.6 cycles. (c) By more: 12 x 29.5 = 354 days, so it would fall short by 400 - 354 = 46 days, compared with about 365 - 354 = 11 days now.
s: (a) only the year changes
(b) about 13.6 cycles
(c) more: 46 days short instead of about 11

questions.q:
(a) The Earth takes nearly a quarter of a day more than 365 days to go round the Sun. How many hours is that quarter day?
(b) Using (a), explain why calendars add one whole day every four years instead of adding the extra hours every year.
questions.a: (a) 24 / 4 = 6 hours. (b) A calendar counts only whole days, so the extra 6 hours cannot be added each year; after four years they add up to 4 x 6 = 24 hours, one whole day, which is added as a leap day.
s: (a) 6 hours
(b) 4 x 6 = 24 hours make one whole day, added every fourth year

questions.q:
A heritage museum in Ujjain builds three 'sky clocks': clock P is an upright stick with a shadow board, clock Q is a chart for matching the Moon's shape each night, and clock R is a chart of the seasons. For each task, choose the clock and explain. (1 mark each)

(ii) Count off about four weeks for a monthly village market.
(iii) Tell farmers when the sowing season comes back.
(iv) Why is clock P read at the shortest shadow, and not at some other length of shadow?
(v) Explain why clock Q alone cannot tell farmers the sowing season year after year.
questions.a: (i) Clock P: a solar day runs from the Sun's highest position to the next, shown by the shortest shadow on successive days. (ii) Clock Q: one cycle of the Moon's phases takes about 29.5 days, nearly four weeks. (iii) Clock R: the seasons repeat once in each revolution of the Earth around the Sun, nearly 365 and a quarter days. (iv) The shadow is shortest when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky, and the day is measured from one highest position of the Sun to the next. (v) Twelve phase cycles are about 354 days, about 11 days short of the cycle of seasons, so the same Moon month falls about 11 days earlier against the seasons each year.
s: (i) clock P, highest Sun to highest Sun
(ii) clock Q, about 29.5 days
(iii) clock R, one cycle of seasons
(iv) shortest shadow marks the single highest-Sun moment
(v) 12 phase cycles are about 11 days short of the seasons

questions.q: Lakshmi's family follows a Purnimant calendar. Does each of their months begin in Shukla Paksha or in Krishna Paksha? Explain.

questions.q: A school is making a 400-year wall chart of the Gregorian calendar. Which of these years should be printed with a 29 February?

Leap year: 21 March + 31 days = 21 April. So 1 Vaisakha is 21 April in both.

Claim 2: 'So a luni-solar calendar adds an extra month every single year.'

questions.a: Partly right. Claim 1 is correct: 12 lunar months make 354 days, about 11 days short of the solar year. Claim 2 is wrong: the extra month (Adhika Maasa) is not added every year. The 11-day shortfall builds up, and only every 2 to 3 years, when the gap comes close to a full month, is the extra month added.

questions.a: True. A lunar year of 12 lunar months is about 354 days, about 11 days shorter than the cycle of seasons, and a purely lunar calendar makes no correction. So its New Year falls about 11 days earlier against the seasons each year and slowly moves through all the seasons.
s: verdict: true
354-day lunar year drifts about 11 days a year against the seasons, with no correction

questions.q: Lata's family follows an Amant calendar. Tonight is Amavasya. What happens in their calendar tomorrow?

questions.q: A club proposes a calendar of 12 months of 30 days each, with no leap days or extra months. Show that it cannot stay in step with the seasons, and find how far off it would be after 10 years.
questions.a: The calendar year is 12 x 30 = 360 days, but the seasons repeat in nearly 365 and a quarter days. So the calendar falls short by 365.25 - 360 = 5.25 days every year, and with no correction this keeps adding up. After 10 years it is off by 10 x 5.25 = 52.5 days, close to two months, so the seasons would arrive in different months.
s: calendar year 360 days against about 365.25 days for the seasons
shortfall of 5.25 days a year keeps adding up with no correction
after 10 years about 52.5 days off

questions.q:
Explain, with numbers, why the Gregorian calendar needs both the leap-year rule and its 100- and 400-year corrections.
(a) How many extra hours does the Earth take each year beyond 365 days, and how does this give one extra day every four years? (1 mark)
(b) The time from one spring equinox to the next is slightly less than 365 and a quarter days. What goes wrong if a day is added every four years without exception? (1 mark)
(c) In a span of 400 years, how many leap years does the simple divisible-by-four rule give, and how many does the full Gregorian rule give? (1 mark)
(d) Classify 1600, 1700, 1800, 1900 and 2000 as leap or not. (1 mark)
(e) Find the average length of a Gregorian year over 400 years and say whether it is more or less than 365.25 days. (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) About a quarter of a day, 6 hours; 4 x 6 = 24 hours, one extra day every four years, added as 29 February. (b) Since the real year is slightly less than 365.25 days, adding a day every four years adds a little too much, and the calendar slowly drifts ahead of the seasons. (c) Simple rule: 400 / 4 = 100 leap years. Gregorian rule: three century years in every four are skipped, so 100 - 3 = 97. (d) 1600 and 2000 are leap years (divisible by 400); 1700, 1800 and 1900 are not (century years not divisible by 400). (e) (400 x 365 + 97) / 400 = 365.2425 days, slightly less than 365.25, matching the slightly shorter equinox-to-equinox year.
s: (a) 6 hours a year, 24 hours in four years
(b) adding every four years adds a little too much
(c) 100 leap years by the simple rule, 97 by the Gregorian rule
(e) 365.2425 days, slightly less than 365.25

questions.q:
In a village, festivals are fixed by the Moon's phases, but farming depends on the seasons.
(a) What two cycles does a luni-solar calendar keep track of at once?
(b) Explain why such a village would choose a luni-solar calendar rather than a purely lunar or a purely solar one.
questions.a: (a) The Moon's phases, used for counting days and months, and the cycle of seasons (the solar year), kept in step by adding an extra month every 2 to 3 years. (b) A purely lunar calendar would keep the festivals on the right Moon phases but drift through the seasons; a purely solar calendar would stay with the seasons but its dates would not match the Moon's phases. The luni-solar calendar keeps both.
s: (a) the Moon's phases and the cycle of seasons
(b) lunar drifts from seasons, solar loses the phases; luni-solar keeps both

questions.q: A government order is dated 1 Chaitra 1950 Saka. The Indian National Calendar began on 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka, which was 21 March 1956. On which Gregorian date was the order issued?

questions.q:
In a luni-solar calendar suppose a festival month falls at the start of the monsoon in Year 1. Twelve lunar months make 354 days.
(a) If no extra month were ever added, how many days earlier against the seasons would that month fall by Year 4 (three years later)? (1 mark)
(b) Why would a luni-solar calendar insert an Adhika Maasa by about then? (1 mark)
(c) After one extra month of about 29.5 days is inserted, how far is the festival month now from its Year 1 position? (1 mark)
(d) In a purely lunar calendar, which never adds a month, about how many years would the festival month take to drift through all the seasons and return to the monsoon? (1 mark)
(e) A farmers' cooperative must choose between a purely lunar calendar and a luni-solar one for fixing its sowing festival. Choose, using your answers. (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) 365 - 354 = 11 days a year, so 3 x 11 = 33 days earlier. (b) The accumulated difference (33 days) has become close to, in fact more than, a full lunar month, so an extra month is inserted to bring the months back in step with the seasons; this is why it happens every 2 to 3 years. (c) 33 - 29.5 = 3.5 days, so it is back within a few days of its Year 1 position. (d) 365 / 11 = about 33 years. (e) The luni-solar calendar: it keeps the festival within about a month of the same season, while in a purely lunar calendar it would move through all the seasons in about 33 years, which is useless for sowing.
s: (a) 33 days earlier
(b) the gap is close to a full month, so Adhika Maasa is added
(c) 3.5 days from the Year 1 position
(d) about 33 years
(e) luni-solar, since it stays within about a month of the season

questions.a: Days from one spring equinox to the next spring equinox

questions.q:
Before 1952, many different calendars were in use in different parts of India.
(a) What did the Calendar Reform Committee set up in 1952 do about this?
(b) The national calendar it recommended came into use on 21 March 1956, not 22 March. Use the leap-year rule to explain why.
questions.a: (a) It examined all the calendars then followed in the country and recommended an accurate and uniform calendar for the whole of India, the Unified National Calendar. (b) 1956 is divisible by four (and is not a century year), so it was a Gregorian leap year; in leap years the national calendar adds a day to Chaitra and its year begins on 21 March.
s: (a) examined all calendars and recommended one accurate, uniform national calendar
(b) 1956 was a leap year, so the year began on 21 March

questions.q:
The almanac committee of a school in Hyderabad is preparing the page for 2028, a Gregorian leap year. It prints the Gregorian calendar beside a local luni-solar calendar. The luni-solar calendar had 12 months last year, but for 2028 it shows 13 months, one of them marked 'Adhika'.
(a) How many days does February 2028 have, and why?
(b) Explain why the luni-solar calendar does not correct itself by adding a single day, as the Gregorian calendar does, but adds a whole month.
(c) About how many days long is the 13-month luni-solar year, compared with its 12-month year?
(d) The school's Founders' Day must fall on a full Moon and in roughly the same season every year. Decide which of the two calendars it should be fixed to, and justify.
questions.a: (a) 29 days: 2028 is divisible by four and is not a century year, so a leap day is added. (b) Its months are counted by the Moon's phases, so a month cannot simply gain a day. The shortfall of about 11 days a year against the solar year is allowed to build up until it is close to a full month, and then a whole extra month is added. (c) 13 x 29.5 = about 383.5 days, against about 354 days for 12 months. (d) The luni-solar calendar. A fixed Gregorian date keeps the season but will not fall on a full Moon each year, because the phases do not repeat on the same Gregorian dates. The luni-solar calendar fixes the day by the Moon's phase and, thanks to the Adhika Maasa, keeps it within less than a month of the same season.
s: (a) 29 days: divisible by four, not a century year
(b) months follow the Moon's phases; the gap builds to about a month before a month is added
(c) about 383.5 days against about 354
(d) luni-solar: keeps the full Moon and stays within a month of the season

questions.q:
A Gregorian calendar follows the tropical year, while astronomers keep track of the Earth's position with the sidereal year, about 20 minutes longer.
(a) Define the tropical year and the sidereal year in terms of what is observed.
(b) How many years does it take for the two to differ by one whole day?
(c) Use (b) to explain why ordinary users of the Gregorian calendar never notice the difference.
questions.a: (a) Tropical year: the time between successive spring equinoxes. Sidereal year: the time for the same stars to rise again at sunset. (b) One day is 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes; 1440 / 20 = 72 years. (c) The difference grows by only one day in about 72 years, so it takes a long time before the two calendars noticeably differ; within a person's everyday use the change is far too small to see.
s: (a) tropical: spring equinox to spring equinox; sidereal: same stars rising at sunset again
(c) only one day in about 72 years, too slow to notice

questions.q:
Consider the statements.

Statement 2: A month in a Purnimant calendar ends on the full Moon day.
Statement 3: In a Gregorian leap year, the Indian National Calendar's year begins on 21 March.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

questions.q:
(a) Why does the Gregorian calendar use months of 30 and 31 days and a 28-day February, instead of months that follow the Moon's phases?
(b) What would slowly go wrong for farmers if February never got a 29th day?
questions.a: (a) It is a solar calendar: its months are adjusted to add up to 365 days so that the year stays in step with the seasons, which matters for agriculture; months following the Moon would make only about 354 days. (b) The Earth takes nearly a quarter day more than 365 days, so without leap days the calendar would slip about one day every four years against the seasons, and sowing dates would gradually drift.

questions.q:
Compare the Moon with a typical artificial satellite. Take the Moon's time to go once around the Earth as 30 days.
(a) How many complete orbits does a typical artificial satellite make in one day? (1 mark)
(b) How many orbits does it make while the Moon goes around the Earth once? (1 mark)
(c) Which of the two is a natural satellite, and what makes the other artificial? (1 mark)
(d) Our month comes from the Moon. Why does the chapter build calendar units on the Moon's cycle rather than on a satellite's orbit? (1 mark)
(e) Which of the two can become space debris, and when? (1 mark)
questions.a: (a) 1440 / 100 = about 14 complete orbits a day (14.4). (b) 30 x 1440 / 100 = 432 orbits. (c) The Moon is natural; an artificial satellite is man-made and launched from the Earth by a country. (d) The Moon's phases are a natural periodic event that anyone can watch in the sky, so people have long counted months by them; an artificial satellite is a recent man-made object seen only as a tiny moving speck, and its orbit is not part of the natural cycles on which calendars were built. (e) Only the artificial satellite: after its useful life it becomes space debris.
s: (a) about 14 orbits a day
(b) 432 orbits
(c) Moon natural; artificial = man-made and launched
(d) Moon's phases are a natural cycle everyone can observe
(e) the artificial satellite, after its useful life
